{{Short description|Calculation of position based on satellite signal timing}}
{{Technical|date=June 2023}}
[[Satellite navigation]] solution for the receiver's position ([[geopositioning]]) involves an algorithm. In essence, a [[GNSS]] receiver measures the transmitting time of GNSS signals emitted from four or more GNSS satellites (giving the [[pseudorange]]) and these measurements are used to obtain its position (i.e., [[Coordinate system|spatial coordinates]]) and reception time.<!--
In essence, from each received satellite signal a single measured quantity is obtained (time of arrival of information from the satellite). Four quantities need to be computed: three spatial coordinates and the absolute time. Thus, it is necessary to receive signals from a minimum of four satellites in order to solve for the four unknowns. With more than four signals available, it is possible to use the extra information to check for consistency and to improve the accuracy of the position and time. -->

The following are expressed in [[inertial frame|inertial-frame]] coordinates.

==Calculation steps==
{{olist
|1= A [[global navigation satellite system|global-navigation-satellite-system]] (GNSS) receiver measures the apparent transmitting time, <math> \tilde{t}_i</math>, or "phase", of GNSS signals emitted from four or more GNSS [[satellite]]s (<math> i = 1,\, 2,\, 3,\, 4,\, ..,\, n</math> ), simultaneously.<ref name="Misra_Enge">Misra, P. and Enge, P.,  Global Positioning System: Signals, Measurements, and Performance, 2nd, Ganga-Jamuna Press, 2006.</ref>
|2= GNSS satellites broadcast the messages of satellites' [[ephemeris]], <math> \boldsymbol{r}_i (t)</math>, and intrinsic clock bias (i.e., clock advance), <math>\delta t_{\text{clock,sv},i} (t)</math>{{clarify|what does 'sv' denote?|date=December 2017}} as the functions of ([[atomic clock|atomic]]) [[standard time]], e.g., [[GPST]].<ref name="IS-GPS">{{Cite web |url=http://www.navcen.uscg.gov/pdf/IS-GPS-200D.pdf |title=The interface specification of NAVSTAR GLOBAL POSITIONING SYSTEM |access-date=2010-07-18 |archive-date=2011-05-16 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110516170432/http://www.navcen.uscg.gov/pdf/IS-GPS-200D.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref>
|3= The transmitting time of GNSS satellite signals, <math> t_i</math>, is thus derived from the non-[[closed-form expression|closed-form]] [[equations]] <math> \tilde{t}_i = t_i + \delta t_{\text{clock},i} (t_i)</math> and <math> \delta t_{\text{clock},i} (t_i) = \delta t_{\text{clock,sv},i} (t_i) + \delta t_{\text{orbit-relativ},\, i} (\boldsymbol{r}_i,\, \dot{\boldsymbol{r}}_i)</math>, where <math> \delta t_{\text{orbit-relativ},i} (\boldsymbol{r}_i,\, \dot{\boldsymbol{r}}_i)</math> is the [[Theory of relativity|relativistic]] clock bias, periodically risen from the satellite's [[orbital eccentricity]] and Earth's [[gravity field]].<ref name="IS-GPS"/>  The satellite's position and velocity are determined by <math> t_i</math> as follows: <math> \boldsymbol{r}_i = \boldsymbol{r}_i (t_i)</math> and <math> \dot{\boldsymbol{r}}_i = \dot{\boldsymbol{r}}_i (t_i)</math>. The satellite's position is derived from <math> \boldsymbol{r}_i = \boldsymbol{r}_i (t_i)</math>.
|4= In the field of GNSS, "geometric range", <math> r(\boldsymbol{r}_A,\, \boldsymbol{r}_B) </math>, is defined as straight range, or 3-dimensional [[distance#Geometry|distance]],{{efn|3-dimensional [[distance#Geometry|distance]] is given by <math> r(\boldsymbol{r}_A,\, \boldsymbol{r}_B) = |\boldsymbol{r}_A - \boldsymbol{r}_B| = \sqrt{(x_A-x_B)^2+(y_A-y_B)^2+(z_A-z_B)^2}</math> where <math> \boldsymbol{r}_A = (x_A, y_A, z_A)</math> and <math>\boldsymbol{r}_B = (x_B, y_B, z_B)</math> represented in [[inertial frame]].}} from <math>\boldsymbol{r}_A</math> to <math>\boldsymbol{r}_B</math> in [[inertial frame]] (e.g., [[Earth-centered inertial|ECI]] one), not in [[rotating frame]].<ref name="IS-GPS"/>
|5= The receiver's position, <math> \boldsymbol{r}_{\text{rec}}</math>,  and reception time, <math>  t_{\text{rec}}</math>, satisfy the [[light-cone]] equation of <math> r(\boldsymbol{r}_i,\, \boldsymbol{r}_{\text{rec}}) / c + (t_i - t_{\text{rec}}) = 0 </math> in [[inertial frame]], where <math> c</math> is the [[speed of light]]. The signal time of flight from satellite to receiver is <math> -(t_i - t_{\text{rec}})</math>.
|6= The above is extended to the [[Global navigation satellite system|satellite-navigation]] [[Real-time locating system|positioning]] [[equation]], <math> r(\boldsymbol{r}_i,\, \boldsymbol{r}_{\text{rec}}) / c + (t_i - t_{\text{rec}}) + \delta t_{\text{atmos},i} - \delta t_{\text{meas-err},i} = 0 </math>, where <math> \delta t_{\text{atmos},i}</math> is [[atmospheric delay]] (= [[ionospheric delay]] + [[tropospheric delay]]) along signal path and <math> \delta t_{\text{meas-err},i}</math> is the measurement error.
|7= The [[Gauss–Newton]] method can be used to solve the [[nonlinear]] [[least-squares problem]] for the solution: <math> (\hat{\boldsymbol{r}}_{\text{rec}},\, \hat{t}_{\text{rec}}) = \arg \min  \phi ( \boldsymbol{r}_{\text{rec}},\,  t_{\text{rec}} )</math>, where <math> \phi ( \boldsymbol{r}_{\text{rec}},\, t_{\text{rec}} ) = \sum_{i=1}^n ( \delta t_{\text{meas-err},i} / \sigma_{\delta t_{\text{meas-err},i} } )^2 </math>. Note that <math> \delta t_{\text{meas-err},i}</math> should be regarded as a function of <math> \boldsymbol{r}_{\text{rec}}</math> and <math> t_{\text{rec}}</math>.
<!-- and <math> \delta t_{\text{meas-err},i} ( \boldsymbol{r}_{\text{rec}},\, t_{\text{rec}} ) = r(\boldsymbol{r}_i,\, \boldsymbol{r}_{\text{rec}}) / c + (t_i - t_{\text{rec}}) + \delta t_{\text{atmos},i}  </math>. -->
<!-- ( \boldsymbol{r}_{\text{rec}},\, t_{\text{rec}} ) -->
<!-- , in order to obtain the solution of the receiver's position, <math> \boldsymbol{r}_{\text{rec}}</math>, and reception time, <math> t_{\text{rec}}</math>. -->
<!-- \underset{(\boldsymbol{r}_{\text{rec}},\, t_{\text{rec}})  }{\arg \min} -->
|8= The [[posterior distribution]] of <math> \boldsymbol{r}_{\text{rec}}</math> and <math> t_{\text{rec}}</math> is proportional to <math> \exp ( -\frac{1}{2} \phi ( \boldsymbol{r}_{\text{rec}},\, t_{\text{rec}} ) )</math>, whose [[Mode (statistics)|mode]] is <math> (\hat{\boldsymbol{r}}_{\text{rec}},\, \hat{t}_{\text{rec}})</math>. Their inference is formalized as [[maximum a posteriori estimation]].
|9= The [[posterior distribution]] of <math> \boldsymbol{r}_{\text{rec}}</math> is proportional to <math> \int_{-\infty}^\infty \exp ( -\frac{1}{2} \phi ( \boldsymbol{r}_{\text{rec}},\, t_{\text{rec}} ) ) \, d t_{\text{rec}}</math>.
}}

===Notes for above===
* In the field of GNSS, <math display="inline">\tilde{r}_i = -c (\tilde{t}_i - \tilde{t}_{\text{rec}})</math> is called [[pseudorange]], where <math display="inline">\tilde{t}_{\text{rec}}</math> is a provisional reception time of the receiver. <math display="inline">\delta t_{\text{clock,rec}} = \tilde{t}_{\text{rec}} - t_{\text{rec}}</math> is called receiver's clock bias (i.e., clock advance).<ref name="Misra_Enge"/>
* Standard GNSS receivers output <math display="inline">\tilde{r}_i</math> and <math display="inline">\tilde{t}_{\text{rec}}</math> per an observation [[Epoch (astronomy)|epoch]].
* The temporal variation in the relativistic clock bias of satellite is linear if its orbit is circular (and thus its velocity is uniform in inertial frame).
* The signal time of flight from satellite to receiver is expressed as <math display="inline">-(t_i - t_{\text{rec}}) = \tilde{r}_i/c + \delta t_{\text{clock},i} - \delta t_{\text{clock,rec}}</math>, whose right side is [[round-off error|round-off-error]] resistive during calculation.
* The geometric range is calculated as <math display="inline">r(\boldsymbol{r}_i,\, \boldsymbol{r}_{\text{rec}}) = |  \Omega_{\text{E}} (t_i - t_{\text{rec}}) \boldsymbol{r}_{i,\text{ECEF}} - \boldsymbol{r}_{\text{rec,ECEF}}  |</math>, where the [[ECEF|Earth-centred, Earth-fixed]] (ECEF) rotating frame (e.g., [[WGS84]] or [[International Terrestrial Reference Frame|ITRF]]) is used in the right side and <math display="inline">\Omega_{\text{E}}</math> is the Earth rotating matrix with the argument of the signal [[time of flight|transit time]].<ref name="IS-GPS"/> The matrix can be factorized as <math display="inline">\Omega_{\text{E}} (t_i - t_{\text{rec}}) = \Omega_{\text{E}} (\delta t_{\text{clock,rec}}) \Omega_{\text{E}} (-\tilde{r}_i/c - \delta t_{\text{clock},i}) </math>.
* The line-of-sight unit vector of satellite observed at <math display="inline">\boldsymbol{r}_{\text{rec,ECEF}}</math> is described as: <math display="inline">\boldsymbol{e}_{i, \text{rec,ECEF}} = -\frac{\partial r(\boldsymbol{r}_i,\, \boldsymbol{r}_{\text{rec}})}{\partial \boldsymbol{r}_{\text{rec,ECEF}}} </math>.
* The [[Global navigation satellite system|satellite-navigation]] [[Real-time locating system|positioning]] [[equation]] may be expressed by using the [[variable (mathematics)|variables]] <math display="inline">\boldsymbol{r}_{\text{rec,ECEF}}</math> and <math display="inline">\delta t_{\text{clock,rec}}</math>.
* The [[nonlinearity]] of the vertical dependency of [[tropospheric delay]] degrades the convergence efficiency in the [[Gauss–Newton]] iterations in step 7.
* The above notation is different from that in the Wikipedia articles, 'Position calculation introduction' and 'Position calculation advanced', of [[Global Positioning System]] (GPS).

== The GPS case ==
{{ulist
|1= For [[Global Positioning System]] (GPS),<ref name="IS-GPS"/> the non-closed-form equations in step 3 result in
<!-- <math display="inline">\Delta t_i (t_i,\, E_i) \equiv t_i + \delta t_{\text{clock},i} (t_i,\, E_i) - \tilde{t}_i = 0</math> and <math display="inline">\Delta M_i (t_i,\, E_i) \equiv M_i (t_i) - (E_i - e_i \sin E_i) = 0</math>, -->
<math display=block> \begin{cases}
  \Delta t_i (t_i,\, E_i) \triangleq t_i + \delta t_{\text{clock},i} (t_i,\, E_i) - \tilde{t}_i = 0, \\
  \Delta M_i (t_i,\, E_i) \triangleq M_i (t_i) - (E_i - e_i \sin E_i) = 0, 
\end{cases} </math>
in which <math display="inline">E_i</math> is the orbital [[eccentric anomaly]] of satellite <math>i</math>, <math display="inline">M_i</math> is the [[mean anomaly]], <math display="inline">e_i</math> is the [[orbital eccentricity|eccentricity]], and <math display="inline">\delta t_{\text{clock},i} (t_i,\, E_i) = \delta t_{\text{clock,sv},i} (t_i) + \delta t_{\text{orbit-relativ},i} (E_i)</math>.
|2=The above can be solved by using the [[bivariate analysis|bivariate]] [[Newton–Raphson]] method on <math display="inline">t_i</math> and <math display="inline">E_i</math>. Two times of iteration will be necessary and sufficient in most cases. Its iterative update will be described by using the approximated [[inverse matrix|inverse]] of [[Jacobian matrix and determinant|Jacobian]] matrix as follows:
<math display="block">
\begin{pmatrix}
  t_i \\
  E_i \\
\end{pmatrix}
\leftarrow 
\begin{pmatrix}
  t_i \\
  E_i \\
\end{pmatrix}
- 
\begin{pmatrix}
  1 & 0 \\
  \frac{\dot{M}_i (t_i)}{1 - e_i \cos E_i} & -\frac{1}{1 - e_i \cos E_i} \\
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
  \Delta t_i \\
  \Delta M_i \\
\end{pmatrix}
</math>
|3=[[Tropospheric delay]] should not be ignored, while the [[Global Positioning System]] (GPS) specification<ref name="IS-GPS"/> doesn't provide its detailed description. <!--mention it clearly.-->
}}

== The GLONASS case ==
* The [[GLONASS]] ephemerides don't provide clock biases <math display=inline>\delta t_{\text{clock,sv},i} (t)</math>, but <math  display=inline>\delta t_{\text{clock},i} (t)</math>.
